61.event_title: Aage Bohr follows his father Niels Bohr to a Nobel Prize in Physics
61.event: Aage Bohr, born in Copenhagen in 1922 as the fourth son of the physicist Niels Bohr, studied physics at the University of Copenhagen and from 1943 to 1945 worked as his father's assistant and secretary. After Niels Bohr's death in 1962 he became director of the institute his father had founded, serving until 1970. In 1975 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Ben Mottelson and James Rainwater for work on the structure of the atomic nucleus.
61.explanation: Niels Bohr's son did not simply inherit his father's name; he mastered the same science and carried it into a new field, becoming a laureate in his own right.
61.tie_back: The kural ranks children who have learned what is worth knowing above every other possession, and the Bohr household's greatest legacy was a son whose own learning matched his father's.
61._accuracy_note: A clear documented case of a learned child carrying on a parent's work, though the sources record the achievement rather than the father's own valuation of it.

62.event_title: Suor Maria Celeste takes on her father Galileo's penance
62.event: In June 1633 the Roman Inquisition condemned Galileo Galilei over his Dialogue on the two chief world systems and imposed a penance that included the repeated recitation of the penitential psalms. His eldest daughter, Suor Maria Celeste, a Poor Clare nun at the convent of San Matteo in Arcetri, took on that part of his penance herself. Throughout his trial she wrote to him constantly and looked after his household affairs while he was away in Rome.
62.explanation: A daughter of good character stood in for her father and shouldered the burden laid on him, one of the best-documented acts of filial devotion in the history of science.
62.tie_back: Parimelalagar reads this kural as saying that a virtuous child's good acts lift the burden from the parent, and Maria Celeste literally performed her father's penance in his place.
62._accuracy_note: Remarkably close to the commentarial reading of a child's merit relieving a parent, though the kural's promise about seven births is beyond what any event can show.

63.event_title: Andrew Carnegie publishes 'Wealth', the Gospel of Wealth
63.place: United States (published in the North American Review)
63.event: In June 1889 the industrialist Andrew Carnegie published an essay titled 'Wealth' in the North American Review, setting out what came to be called the Gospel of Wealth. He argued that a person who accumulates great wealth holds it as a trustee and should use the surplus for the improvement of mankind during his own lifetime, and he questioned the practice of passing great fortunes down to heirs. Carnegie went on to give away the great majority of his fortune to libraries, universities and foundations.
63.explanation: One of the richest men of his age publicly argued that children are not best served by inherited riches, and that each person's standing should come from what they themselves do.
63.tie_back: The kural says children are a parent's true wealth while their own wealth must come through their own deeds, which is close to Carnegie's case against handing heirs great fortunes.
63._accuracy_note: Matches the kural's second line on wealth earned by one's own deeds well, but says little about children as the parent's own treasure.

64.event_title: Victor Hugo publishes The Art of Being a Grandfather
64.event: After his son Charles died in 1871, Victor Hugo took charge of the upbringing of his two young grandchildren, Georges and Jeanne. In May 1877 he published L'Art d'etre grand-pere (The Art of Being a Grandfather), a collection of poems devoted to the two children and their everyday play. The book was a great success, and Georges and Jeanne became famous through it.
64.explanation: France's most celebrated poet, near the end of a career spent on epic and political themes, chose small children and their ordinary doings as the subject of one of his last collections.
64.tie_back: The kural says the plain food a child's little hands have stirred is sweeter than the nectar of the gods, and Hugo set the small daily doings of his grandchildren above the grand themes of his earlier work.
64._accuracy_note: Captures the delight in small children's ordinary acts, but concerns grandchildren and poetry rather than the specific image of a shared meal.

65.event_title: Kangaroo mother care is developed in Bogota
65.event: Facing a shortage of incubators and high infection rates among low birth weight babies, the Colombian paediatricians Edgar Rey Sanabria and Hector Martinez-Gomez began in 1978 to have mothers carry their premature infants in continuous skin-to-skin contact on their chests. The method, combined with breastfeeding and early discharge, became known as the Kangaroo Mother Program. It was later studied internationally, and the World Health Organization published guidelines on kangaroo mother care in 2003.
65.explanation: Doctors found that a parent's touch, not only machines, could keep the most fragile newborns warm and help them thrive, and the practice spread around the world.
65.tie_back: The kural calls the touch of one's child the body's delight, and kangaroo care made that very touch, skin to skin, into a recognised form of medicine for both mother and baby.
65._accuracy_note: A strong documented case of parent-child touch being valued, though the motive was medical survival rather than the parent's delight the kural describes.

66.event_title: Charles Darwin records his infant son's first expressions and sounds
66.event: From the birth of his first child, William Erasmus, on 27 December 1839, Charles Darwin kept a notebook recording the baby's movements, cries, smiles and responses to sounds, and he continued the observations for several years. The notes later fed into his 1872 book on the expression of emotions. In 1877 he drew on them for the article A biographical sketch of an infant, published in the journal Mind.
66.explanation: The great naturalist turned the same patient attention he gave to finches and barnacles on his own baby, and the Darwin Correspondence Project notes the obvious pride and joy that shows through the notes.
66.tie_back: The kural says those who rank the flute and lute sweetest have never heard their own child's babble, and Darwin, among the most observant minds of his age, found his infant's first sounds worth recording for decades.
66._accuracy_note: Shows a father deeply absorbed in his infant's early sounds and expressions, but the record is scientific rather than a comparison with music.

67.event_title: Philip II of Macedon engages Aristotle as tutor to Alexander
67.event: King Philip II of Macedon summoned the philosopher Aristotle to act as tutor to his 13-year-old son Alexander. Aristotle taught the prince for about three years, from roughly age 13 to 16. Ancient tradition, reported by Plutarch, places the lessons at Mieza, where archaeologists have excavated a complex believed to be the school.
67.explanation: Philip, already a powerful king, judged that the best thing he could give his heir was the finest teacher in the Greek world.
67.tie_back: The kural defines a father's duty as making his son fit to sit in the front rank of the learned, and Philip secured for Alexander the most learned tutor of the age.
67._accuracy_note: A close illustration of a father investing in his son's education, though Alexander became famous as a conqueror rather than as a scholar.

68.event_title: Leopold Mozart sets aside his own career to train Wolfgang
68.place: Salzburg, Austria, and courts across Europe
68.event: Leopold Mozart was a court musician in Salzburg and the author of a 1756 violin method that became a standard text and was widely translated. In the years after his son Wolfgang was born in 1756, he largely, though not entirely, gave up composing in order to teach his two gifted children, Nannerl and Wolfgang, and took them on long concert tours across Europe. Wolfgang went on to surpass his father completely as a composer.
68.explanation: A respected musician deliberately made room for a child whose gifts exceeded his own, and the son's music became a lasting pleasure for listeners all over the world.
68.tie_back: The kural says that a child wiser than the parent delights not only the parents but every living being on earth, and Wolfgang's surpassing of Leopold produced music the whole world still enjoys.
68._accuracy_note: An unusually exact fit: a child outshining an accomplished parent, with the benefit spreading far beyond the family.

69.event_title: Einstein sends his ailing mother news that his theory has been confirmed
69.event: In September 1919 Albert Einstein learned by telegram from the physicist H. A. Lorentz that British eclipse expeditions had confirmed the bending of starlight by the Sun predicted by his general theory of relativity. He at once sent a postcard with the good news to his mother, Pauline, who was seriously ill, and in the same card wished he could keep her company. Einstein became world-famous after the results were announced in November 1919, and his mother, whom he brought to his Berlin home at the end of that year, died there in February 1920.
69.explanation: In the last months of her life, a mother heard that her son had been proved right before the whole scientific world.
69.tie_back: The kural says a mother's joy on hearing her son called a person of true worth exceeds her joy at his birth, and Pauline Einstein lived just long enough to hear her son acclaimed.
69._accuracy_note: The mother hearing of her son's vindication is well documented, though her own reaction is not recorded, so the joy itself is inferred.

70.event_title: Dorabji Tata completes his father Jamsetji's steel works
70.event: Jamsetji Tata began planning India's first large-scale iron and steel works in the early 1900s but died in Germany in May 1904. His elder son Dorabji carried the project forward, and the Tata Iron and Steel Company was incorporated in 1907, with a plant and township built at the village of Sakchi. In 1919 the township was renamed Jamshedpur in Jamsetji's honour.
70.explanation: The son's work kept his father's name at the centre of the achievement, so that a whole city came to be named after the father.
70.tie_back: The kural says a son repays his father by living so that people ask what the father did to deserve such a son, and Dorabji's work made Jamsetji's name permanent in the city of Jamshedpur.
70._accuracy_note: A good case of a son's achievement bringing honour to his father's name, though the credit is shared with Dorabji's cousin Ratanji and many others.
